h1: Box and pan brakes — finger brakes from 12″ to 13 ft, 22 to 12 gauge
intro: A box and pan brake (finger brake) is a sheet metal brake whose upper clamping blade is made of removable fingers: take the fingers out where the sides of a box come up and the leaf folds all four sides of a box or a pan; with every finger in place it works as a straight brake. NovoTech sells three kinds in Canada, all on this page: hand-operated box and pan brakes from a 12″ bench model to 157″, in 22 to 12 ga; heavy box and pan brakes from 52 to 100″ with 2, 3 and 4″ fingers that fold 14 ga boxes 9″ deep; and hydraulic box and pan brakes that clamp and fold 14 ga over 52 and 100″ from a foot pedal. Every model is listed in one table below with its length, capacity and weight, then each family with its full specification, photos and the finger sets supplied. NovoTech's value-line brakes are built in China to our specification, with parts and support from Mississauga, ON, Canada.

faq.q: Box and pan brake or straight hand brake?
faq.a: A straight (hand) brake has a one-piece clamping blade: the best choice for long straight bends such as flashing, trim and duct panels, and a little stiffer for its length. A box and pan brake has a blade of removable fingers, so it also folds the four sides of a box or a pan; with all the fingers in place it does everything the straight brake does. Most shops that make boxes, pans, enclosures and ducts buy the box and pan brake; the straight brakes are on the hand brake page.

faq.q: How deep a box can I fold?
faq.a: The box depth is limited by the height of the fingers and the clearance behind the clamping beam: the standard box and pan brakes fold boxes up to about the finger height (2 – 3″), the heavy brakes with 4″ fingers fold 14 ga boxes 9″ deep, and for boxes of any depth a magnetic brake — which has no beam frame at the ends — is the machine. The maximum depth per model is in the specification table.

faq.q: How are the capacities rated, and what about stainless and aluminum?
faq.a: Capacities are given in gauge of mild steel over the full bending length. Stainless steel bends at about two gauges lighter (a 16 ga brake takes 20 ga stainless), aluminum at about two gauges heavier. Bending at less than full length lets a brake take somewhat heavier sheet; folding heavier material than rated bends the beams permanently.

faq.q: Which finger sets come with the machine?
faq.a: A full set of fingers that adds up to the bending length is in the crate, in widths from 1″ to 6″ (2, 3 and 4″ on the heavy brakes), so any combination of box sides can be made; extra fingers and narrow 1/2″ fingers are available. Fingers are hardened and ground on the bending edge and can be reversed for a second edge.

faq.q: Can a brake fold painted or coated sheet without marking it?
faq.a: Yes — that is one of the reasons to fold instead of press-brake bending. The sheet is clamped and the leaf swings around the clamp edge without sliding over a die; a strip of protective film on the sheet keeps pre-painted and stainless finishes perfect.

faq.q: What voltage do these machines run on?
faq.a: Three-phase machines are supplied for 600 V as standard with a CSA-approved panel; 208 V, 240 V and 480 V 3-phase are available on request, and 240 V single-phase on models whose main motor is 2.2 kW (3 HP) or less — a machine with a motor above 2.2 kW must run on three-phase power and cannot be converted to 240 V single-phase. Manual machines have no electrics.
